utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 2 you said that on the 25th of March, 1999, that the army surrounded your village with tanks and armoured vehicles. Where did you see those tanks and armoured vehicles?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We saw them around the village and at the entry points to the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And where were you standing at the time?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI [Resumed]
utterances.text: At 5.00 in the morning I was woken up by my family and told me that they could hear shots. Because I was the elder of the village, I went to the centre of the village near the school to see what was going on there. At 5.30 in the morning, the tank entered the village from the direction of Bellacerke, right at the entrance to the village, about 200 metres from the mosque in the Bellacerke direction. On the opposite direction, Rahovec and Nagavc, there was another position where the tanks and the army were. On the main road, Prizren-Gjakova, there were APCs and the shots were coming from there. This is what I saw when I went out of my house and went towards the centre of the village. Everybody was upset, worried. I spoke to people and then I went back to my house. This is when I saw the tanks and the other cars that were positioned at the entrance of the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said it was 5.00 a.m.?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Was the sun already out? Had day broken?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was normal light. I don't know whether the sun had come up or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: So on the 25th of March, at 5.00 a.m., it's already daylight, is it?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. It's the same time of the year as now, and about 4.30 in the morning or 5.00 a.m. it dawns. There is daylight.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And you saw all those tanks in daylight and those armoured vehicles?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jemini. Well, we can't establish that by talking about whether it's daylight at 5.00 a.m. or not and what could be seen and what could not. We'll establish that through other means. Then you go on to say that the Serb forces attacked the village. Did anybody put up resistance in the village?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what resistance you have in mind. This was a civilian population. There was no army there. The population didn't have any weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Well, how did you know that the population didn't have any weapons?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you think that a tank is equal to an automatic rifle or a rifle, then you must be wrong. I know very well as the elder and responsible for organising the life of the villagers, I know very well that at the time there were no weapons, and there was no defence of the village organised.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: You said that there were no tanks though. You said that the villagers did not have any tanks. Now, how do you know that they didn't have any other weapons?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I am the leader of the village, I should be aware of what the villagers have. As -- to the same effect, I knew very well what was inflicted by the Serb forces on the villagers. You know, the villagers would inform me. Had we been armed, the Serb forces would have suffered casualties and damages, and this is the best argument that we didn't have any weapons to offer them any resistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: In that same paragraph you go on to say that there were no KLA members in the village. What is the KLA? Could you tell me?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The KLA was a unit or an organisation that came out of the people as an organised defence for the civilian population. They would go out to those places where the Serb forces would launch offensive. There was no KLA in our village because there was no intervention on the part of the Serb forces on our village. So there was no need to defend our village. Therefore, in Celine there was no defence organised in the village to oppose the Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And how do you know what you've just told us? How do you know about all that?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean by saying "all that"? What is "all that"?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Your entire previous answer, what the KLA was, what kind of organisation, who it protected, how it offered protection, and everything else that you presented to us here just a moment ago in your answer.

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI [Resumed]
utterances.text: From previous experiences. From the 25th of March and a year earlier. In those places where the Serb forces would launch offensives, the KLA would emerge in order to protect the population. They would have these protective units. This was like an automatic response to the offensives launched by the Serb forces. This was not the case with our village, however, because the police entered the village only on the 25th of March, not earlier, and therefore there was no reason to organise any defend of the village. The village was not attacked earlier. The police and the army encircled the village early in the morning and afterwards entered the village on the 25th. I would like to ask you a question. What was the reason for the intervention of the Serb army and police in the village on the 25th of March when we were just civilians? We didn't cause anyone any harm or damage. We lived our lives quietly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jemini, well, I'll ask my questions on the basis of your answers. Do you know that Celine, for example, had a third-level of fortification or third-degree fortification and that there was fighting in the direction of Bela Crkva to the entrance of Celine on the 25th of March?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI [Resumed]
utterances.text: What was the date?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: The 25th of March, 1999.

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no fighting whatsoever. There was no resistance offered by the population of Celine on the 25th of March. The offensive began in 3.00 or 4.00 in the morning in Bellacerke. They massacred in Bellacerke. They completed their operation there and then advanced in the direction of Celine. After they had finished their job in Bellacerke, they advanced in the direction of Celine, entered Celine, and did what they did to the population of Celine. If you have any knowledge that there was resistance, then I would like you to inform me; but I'm more than [Realtime transcript read in error "almost"] positive that there was no resistance whatsoever offered from our village.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And how do you know about the events in Bela Crkva then?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Behar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Sorry for the interruption. I just noticed that the interpretation at line 16 says almost positive. I believe he said more than positive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jemini, did you hear my question? How do you know what happened in Bela Crkva on the 25th of March, 1999?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the morning of the 25th of March, I was informed about the intervention of the Serb forces in Celine but not about the massacres committed by the police in the evening. Two days later, on the 27th, when I came back from Celine to Zrze, I noticed the corpses between Zrze and Celine. I came across 40 bodies. And in Zrze I was informed about the events of the 25th of March that occurred in Bellacerke village.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 3 you state that at 5.30 the shelling started, and the shooting, in the village. So where was the shooting? Can you tell us? Where did that take place?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI [Resumed]
utterances.text: At around 5.30 in the morning and until 7.00 in the evening, from all four sides you could hear shooting and shelling uninterruptedly. It resembled a war between two fronts, between two armed states and not between an army and unarmed civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jemini. How do you know that most of the elderly women and the children gathered together in one group?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I -- as I visited the centre of the village at around 5.00 in the morning, I returned to my house, and my family, my relatives, close and distance -- distant relatives gathered in a place in the village. I took them there. We left the women, children, and elderly there, and we returned to the position that I mentioned earlier in the house where we were. I positioned myself there at around 6.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I apologise, but I didn't understand where you took the women and the children.

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We took them to a location in the centre of the village. It was an open space. It was like a meadow. It seemed to be a safer place for the population of the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what about the others? Did the other people bring the -- the women and children to the centre of the village and then leave them there?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The whole village. In addition to the 2.000 inhabitants of the village, there were people from other villages who had fled to our village, staying as guests with acquaintances and families.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You then go on to say in that same paragraph, paragraph 3, that people who were younger, between the ages of 18 and 40, that the men stayed to one side. Where was it that they stayed? How do you mean stayed away, stayed to one side?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Knowing the aim of the Serb police and army forces, the men of the age 18 and 40, in order to avoid any ill-treatment of their family members, would stay aside and not amongst the group of women, children, and elderly. They didn't have one specific position to go to. They stayed in different places, just like myself and my uncle's son did. We found this position in that house. So there was no like pre-agreed congregation place.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So the two of you hid. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what about the men between the ages of 18 and 14 [as interpreted]? Were they able-bodied men?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI [Resumed]
utterances.text: You could find a small number of people who were not able-bodied men, but the others were healthy and able-bodied men.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Well, did you think you would be safer in hiding?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see any logic in your question, because we thought we would escape death if we hid. Hiding was safer for us. It was means to avoid risk and danger. And many people survived after they hid. I mean, those people who didn't leave. However, those who did not leave their houses and who did not go in hiding were killed. They were -- their bodies were charred, massacred. These were younger men of the age of 25, 30, 40, 50. So all those people who did not leave their houses and who did not go into hiding suffered consequences. They were killed in their own homes. And I think the same thing would have happened to us, too, if we didn't go into hiding.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Well, you could have been outside with your families, your wives and children.

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI [Resumed]
utterances.text: After 50 years of pressure from the Serb authorities, we knew very well that young men would be targeted, would be massacred and killed. That's -- that's why we thought we wouldn't be safe amongst the women, the elderly, and the children. And that they would not be safe amongst us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And if there was no -- had no -- if there had been nobody in the houses, then there would be no reason for the shooting; right? Am I right in saying that? Had the houses been empty.

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm very sorry that we have to explain this plan of Serb forces and their offensives. We all know how these offensives and plans were carried out. All the noises, all the attacks carried out on the first day, were carried out in order to secure and enforce their position, the positions of the Serb forces so they can later massacre and kill the population. On the 25th and the 26th of March, the people were removed and went to the position that we spoke about. The village was empty. There was no one there. Those that they found in their houses, they killed them, massacred them. So the house was -- the village, correction -- was empty, and the police and the army had full control of the village because they had positions at every entry point to the village. Up until the moment the Kumanovo Agreement was signed, nobody could return to his or her village. They carried out this ethnic cleansing. The police had control of these villages. They looted them, burnt them, and they could easily see and detect any presence in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, I concluded that you knew of the plan in advance.

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to the plan of the Serb army or of the plan of my population?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Tell me about the plan of your people first, the population.

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The population had its duty to leave -- to live quietly, to stay in their homes in case of offensives, to gather on one spot. Nobody planned to leave the village or to go to Albania. Nobody thought of this ethnic cleansing, of this massacre, of this 96 per cent destruction in the village and of this massacre of the population. Forty-five per cent of the population were massacred. So the population could not envisage all this, but the Serb forces and their leadership could. They did have a plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And what about the KLA?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we managed to explain the issue of the army. Had there been army presence in the village, the -- the -- nothing would have happened. The fact that they destroyed, they killed in the village, proves the opposite to your point. Do you have anything that would prove that we caused the Serb forces any damage or any casualty? We lived quietly, minded our own business until the 25th of March. There was nothing going on in the village. We minded our own work and business. We lived if our own houses. As the elder in the village, I was very upset. It was very difficult for me to understand how children -- how a child can be killed, how an elderly man or woman can be killed, let alone en masse killing. We can never forget throughout history what happened. Within two months, I personally had to bury 78 bodies, massacred, charred bodies of civilians, innocent civilians killed without any reason. I simply cannot imagine how something like this can be done. I've travelled a lot in Serbia and Yugoslavia, had contacts with different people, intellectuals, and I really feel embarrassed on behalf of a Serb who lived in Kosova for things that the Serbs committed, because this was totally inhumane. Imagine this: I had to watch the execution of my parents and could do nothing to stop that. And many co-villagers suffered the same thing. I really cannot understand. How can a human being do what they did? I had many Serb colleagues, many Serb contacts. I travelled through the whole territory of Yugoslavia, had contacts with different enterprises, but I can hardly compare what I saw and met during these trips to what happened in Kosova, and that really worried me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Now I would like to ask you to give me specific answers to my questions. You provided me with a lengthy answer, but you didn't give me what I was asking for.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I think that it's time for our technical break, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will have the second break now and resume at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 4 of your statement of the 17th of July, you say that the infantry started advancing towards the village on foot in rows four deep. Where did you see those soldiers?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw the soldiers from the window on the asphalted road Prizren-Gjakova. There were trucks that unloaded the soldiers, and they came from that direction towards the village. I also saw them at 5.30 in the morning when I went towards the centre of the village, because from the village its geographical position allows you to see everything around.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please answer my questions directly. Now you mentioned some things that we have already gone through. In order to be able to complete your examination as soon as possible. Am I right that the soldiers wore green-brown camouflage uniforms?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Am I right when I say that you were able to observe the insignia of the double-headed eagle, the Yugoslav double-headed eagle?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At what distance were the soldiers when you saw them?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 7 to 8 metres from the roof to the road Celine -- of Celine-Krusha.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter is not sure about the distance, whether 7, 8 metres or 70 or 80 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Celine-Krusa road or what about Celine-Krusa?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the junction in the direction of Bellacerke, the road is only 4 to -- 5 to 6 metres from the roof, and from there I could see the movement of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yet we didn't see the road on any of the pictures.

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In one of the previous pictures, the one where you could see the school, the road is visible there. If you put up that photograph, I can show you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 5 you say that you saw 35 soldiers break the gate to your farm; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And on the pictures that we saw today, we actually didn't see the gate.

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The gate was open. You could not see the gate, but the soldiers entered and went into the houses. They also went to my cousin's house. Then we also could see the house where the commanders were stationed. From the place we were hiding, we could see the movements of the army during the whole day.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jemini, please answer my question. Don't now go repeating your statement which I have and the Trial Chamber has and the Prosecution has. So just answer my question. Did those soldiers broke down the gate to your yard? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So the gate had been closed.

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That gate was not locked. It was not locked. However, they still broke it down.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jemini, how can a gate that is closed but unlocked be broken down?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what they did, the soldiers that were present there. In normal circumstances, you open the door -- or the gate normally. In that instance, they broke it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And how did they break it down? Can you please describe it?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This gate, which was the big one, which is 3 metres high, it has a smaller entrance which can be opened. They broke the part around that small door. I could hear them. I could not see them, but I could hear them because they were very close to the place where I was. And then I saw them when they entered the yard.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 6 you say that you recognised the soldiers from Orahovac; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And from the window where you were, you say that you were able to observe the soldiers enter the houses all over the village?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We saw many soldiers that entered the houses in the village. Of course we did not see each and every one of them, but the result was that there was burning and flames and smoke coming out of those houses. So they had been there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And then you go on to say that you saw 12 houses being set on fire during that day.

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: In what part of the village were those houses?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the upper part of the village, between the mosque and the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 9 you say that the commanders who entered the house next to which you were used the balcony of the second floor. Can you say in what direction did this balcony face?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The balcony faced the -- towards the west on the side of the Celine-Krusha road. It was in front of the window where I was at.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yes, but the balcony is at 90-degree angle to the window where you were, to the right. So if you're standing on the balcony and if you're facing straight on the balcony, what can you see? What is it that you face?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. However, the position where we were at the window and the position of the house in front of us 12 metres away where these members of the army were, the commanders were, they were facing each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jemini, when you go out onto the balcony in the house where the soldiers were, your window is to the left; and if the person on the balcony does not turn in any direction, where is that person then looking at? What is the person looking at?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The person could -- can see the land or the part in front of the house. The person can look at the window where I was at, and the person can look in three different directions from the balcony.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'm asking you for just one direction. So what is this person looking at in front of them? I'm not asking what's to the left or what's to the right, but I'm asking you what is straight ahead.

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can see the house we were living in and my cousin's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Very well. Did you see any radio stations that they used?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did have radio equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And did you see such radio stations when you did your national service in the army?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Radio equipment existed at the time when I did my military service, but at that time I did not deal with them. I saw these commanders use these radios. However, you must know that it was very difficult for us to observe freely what kind of equipment they had in their hand, because we were in danger.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you see the radio station?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw the equipment in their hand, but I did not analyse what kind of equipment it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And did they have anything on their heads?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, just military uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: So they didn't have any headphones?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know what an R-U-P is?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: You didn't see a RUP or R-U-P in the army when you were there?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember ever seeing one. I worked in an office.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 10 you say that the commanders used a special code, and it was difficult to understand their orders. Can I then conclude that you didn't understand what it is that they were saying?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Considering the situation we were in, we could not really follow the conversation, every single word of it. However, we could hear something, especially in one of these calls. They mentioned 444, and I think I explained in my statement what I heard. They spoke about the situation on the ground. They had several such conversations. One of these occasions was around 1700 hours when I heard, "What's the situation like in Celine?" I heard them saying, "Is it the same as in Recak?" And the answer was, "Twice as much as Recak." We learned then what had happened or what would happen. We were scared, so scared, because we thought that many more people would die in the next days. We were in shock. Around 1900 hours there was this request to stop the offensive and the shooting and the shelling in Celine. At that moment, the offensive was stopped and there was no other shooting heard. This is what I could observe.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So you claim that you heard the people that they talked to as well?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And you've repeated today, as you said yesterday, that at 1900 hours, when the action was supposed to stop, that it did stop. And in paragraph 14 you say that the shooting went on throughout the night.

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The daylight offensive, the one launched from the morning until evening, was stopped, whereas the positions around the village would intervene every now and then for their own safety during the evening; but the daylight offensive stopped, and the majority of soldiers that were inside the village left. However, you could hear from two or three different positions gun-fire at various time intervals.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: You say that the soldiers took positions at different points in the village. Now, what positions did you see?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first position was at the entry to the village, the junction. The second position was in the direction of Krusha e Madhe, at the entrance to the village. You could hear gun-fire from that position too. The third position was at the school. These were the positions of the night of the 25th, the ones that we observed, positions that were manned by them and from where we heard gun-fire during the night.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So those were the positions they took up at night, and during the night you saw them there at those positions; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how you interpret this verb "see." We could hear the gun-fire from -- coming from these two or three different positions. We didn't go to tour these positions and greet them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And you could also see that there were 20 to 30 soldiers at each of these positions. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI [Resumed]
utterances.text: You could hear the noise, which indicated that there was a group of people. Now, whether there were 20 or 30 of them, that we didn't know, but we just assumed that it should be a group of approximately that number of soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 15, you say that your parents and three other family members went home on the 26th of March, 1999, at around 8.00. Did you come down from the attic when they arrived?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And did you talk to any of your family members?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Who did you talk to and where?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI [Resumed]
utterances.text: My father came to that house first. He came to the floor where we were, to the attic, and explained what had happened on the 25th in the area where they were staying. Then he left. He returned to the basement where the others were staying. Later on, after some time, my mother came to the place where we were. She brought me some food. And despite my request for them to go back to my wife and children, they didn't. I actually refused to eat the food that my mother brought as a sign of protest. My mother was begging me to leave, not to put my life in danger, and left, went back to the basement where my father and my uncle, my uncle's son and his wife were. As she was leaving and going back to the basement, about 10 or 15 minutes away -- metres away from the house where we were, from the road, Celine-Krusha e Madhe, a truck came with paramilitaries or Serb policemen with red head scarves, beards, shaven heads --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I do apologise, but we're wasting valuable time. I asked you a question and now you're going on to recount your statement further. Now, your father, what did he say? Where had they been the previous day?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had been to the location where we had taken them to the previous day together with the other people from the village, the location near the centre of the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned a moment ago, although I didn't ask you that, you mentioned that a military vehicle passed by with 12 specials in it, special force men in it. Can you describe the vehicle?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a military truck, open, without a cover sheet, and there were soldiers on it, standing.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: The truck was moving and didn't stop. Am I right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And in your statement you go on to describe what they looked like, what kind of uniforms they had, so we'll move on. And in passing, they were talking to your mother, as you say in paragraph 17. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, but with their constant movement in the direction of Krusha --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... right in saying that from the place you were in the attic you heard the conversation, you heard them talking?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just tell me where your mother was when this event with the truck took place, this moving truck.

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI [Resumed]
utterances.text: She was between the house where we were and the house opposite to us by the road. About 10 or 12 metres far from our position.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 18, am I right in saying that you state that around 9.00 in the village there were about 2 to 300 soldiers?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And in paragraph 19 you go on to say that about 9.30 a.m., about 30 soldiers entered your yard?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And then in paragraph 20 you say that the soldiers asked your father in Serbian if he had any money.

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And heard all that from the window you were standing at?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And then the soldiers forced your parents and relatives to move towards the gate and then found themselves between two houses. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Jemini, these are all parts of your statement, and at no point did you make any mention of the police or any paramilitaries, whereas yesterday, in response to a question from my learned friend Mr. Behar, you just talked about paramilitaries and some police force that I didn't understand what it was, but it would appear that it wasn't the real police force. Now, how come all this difference between the 17th of July, 1999, what you said there, and what you told us yesterday? Why all this discrepancy?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Djurdjic, but if you look on page -- the page you're on of the statement, in English, the first full paragraph at the top mentions special forces police, describes them, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in my version the vehicle with 12 specials, it says: "At that moment I noticed that some soldiers were approaching the village from the direction of the main road. Within ten minutes I noted -- noticed a vehicle with 12 specials." "Specials," not police. Just specials. And they were the soldiers who talked to his mother, and that was the passing truck. And the first time that he mentions the police is in paragraph 25 when he came back from Zrze. That is to say two or three days later. And in paragraph 28 when the bodies were being collected up, and I'll come to that in due course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That's not in respect of the English translation. There's a mention and a description of the special forces police and a description on how they were armed and, "As they were driving past my house, they saw my mother in our yard," is the beginning of the next paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I can see that now. It says special forces police. Even if that were the case, they were soldiers passing by in the truck. In all the previous paragraphs, exclusive mention is made of the army, soldiers. Nowhere is the police mentioned. So even these men passing by in the truck didn't stop by his house but were passing by.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: If we leave aside the paragraph 16 where this word "police" is mentioned, on that 25th and 26th no mention is made by you, Witness, of the police anywhere there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The next paragraph, I'm afraid, does go on commencing at about -- "Within half an hour, which is about 9.00 a.m., 2 to 300 soldiers in the village; there were groups amongst them that had red ribbons like the men that I had seen in the truck. Some groups had white ribbons. Some groups had headbands around their heads. Some headbands were red. Some were patterned mainly red or black. They were all carrying long knives. They went from house to house." Now, it may be that you will need to clarify what the witness was intending to saying, but I don't believe you're able to say from this statement that there is no mention or no description that could be of police or special forces police, which is the fuller description given in the first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jemini, you described to us the soldiers who were on the truck, in the truck. Now, had you ever seen any soldiers like that before anywhere?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, how were you able to conclude that they were Special Police Forces or special forces police as it says in the English version of your statement in paragraph 16?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that in my statement I described the method applied on the 25th of March and the following days. We could tell the members of the Serbian army because we saw them every day. However, these paramilitaries who carried out the burning, the massacres, and so on, they were different. They wore different kinds of uniforms. They had ribbons. They had beards. They had shaven heads. This is how we could tell that they were different from the regular army.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jemini, you've just said that the first time you saw these soldiers was when they were passing by in the truck on the 26th of March and that you hadn't seen them before that. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not before the 25th of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 16, your introductory sentence was this: "I noticed that the military was approaching the village from the direction of the main road."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel repeat his question after that, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yes. In paragraph 16, you say that some soldiers from the main road was approaching the village -- were approaching the village. What uniforms were those soldiers wearing, the ones who were approaching the village?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Green and black, dark pattern of camouflage uniforms usually worn by the regular army.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in paragraph 18 you say: "At about 9.00 there were 2 to 300 soldiers in the village." What uniforms were those soldiers wearing?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already described that. On the second day, the 26th of March, there were soldiers, there were paramilitaries in addition to the regular army of the previous day. There were different sorts of groups. I mentioned this. Twelve persons on the truck. And there were other persons who came with blue clothes, and there were policemen who were wearing regular police uniforms. And in addition to these different groups, there were these people with beards, shaven heads, with white -- correction, red headscarves and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But in paragraph 19 you say that: "About 30 soldiers at 9.30 entered my yard."

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Seven or eight soldiers came in the direction of the house where we were. Seven or eight others went to the basement where my parents were sheltering. Others went to the house of my uncle, and there were seven, eight, or ten others who stayed the whole day in the house next to the house where we were. So I know that there were around 30 or more than that now. We can maybe count them and come up with a exact figure, but this was the approximate figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, did you see your parents and relatives when the soldiers took them to between the two houses?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Between which two houses were they taken?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the upper part of the house we inhabited. Immediately behind that one. Next to the wall which was alongside the main road.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. "So they took us closer to the fence of the yard." Right? Or the wall.

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that the soldiers left your yard. What time was that?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did not leave during the day. They only left after they committed the execution. They, however, stayed all day at the junction. And during the whole night and the morning on the 17th of March, they still were at the junction. Correction, 27th of March they still were at that junction.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jemini, my question was: When did the soldiers leave your yard? At what time?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 12.00 midnight, 26th of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And there was no nobody left in your compound, no soldiers left in your compound after that?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but there were soldiers at the junction and on the road immediately beyond the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: When you came down from the roof, you passed by the place where your parents and relatives had been?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Did you go up to them?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I didn't dare to, because the police and the army were very close, and because we were afraid, and because we were exhausted. We went round the place -- around the houses. My house, my uncle's house. Because it was very dangerous, because we knew that if we -- if we were seen by them we would be executed. We didn't stop. We just went on towards Zrze.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jemini, you said that the gypsies and the police collected up the bodies of your parents and relatives and that they had been taken away from that place where you saw that they were, the place they were at before and that you went to; right?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, do you remember what you told the German forensic team when you talked to them on the 21st of October, 1999?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Djurdjic, we must stop you there. We've let you run on six or seven minutes to try and find a logical place for you to pause. Perhaps you can take up that subject tomorrow when we continue. We would point out that you had virtually the whole day today in cross-examination. I don't need to say more, I'm sure. You must be very near the end of your cross-examination. We adjourn now and continue tomorrow. I'm afraid, Mr. Jemini, we must adjourn again and ask you to return tomorrow to finish your evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 23rd day of April, 2009, at 9.00 a.m. 17 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
